questionText: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?
option1: A class should have only one reason to change
option2: Objects of a superclass/interface should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking the correctness of the program
option3: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification
option4: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules
correctOptionExplanation: LSP states that any subtype must be substitutable for its base type wherever the base type is expected, without altering the correctness of the program.

questionText: Which SOLID letter does LSP represent?
option1: L
option2: I
option3: S
option4: D
correctOptionExplanation: LSP is the 'L' in SOLID.

questionText: Who is LSP named after?
option1: Barbara Liskov
option2: Robert C. Martin
option3: Martin Fowler
option4: Bertrand Meyer
correctOptionExplanation: The principle is named after computer scientist Barbara Liskov who introduced the substitutability idea in 1987.

questionText: From the course notes, a single `Shape` interface declares both `getArea()` and `getVolume()`. Which classes implement it?
option1: Only Circle and Square
option2: Line, Circle, Rectangle, Square, Sphere, Cuboid — every shape, 1D through 3D
option3: Only Line
option4: Only Sphere and Cuboid
correctOptionExplanation: The notes show one fat Shape interface being implemented by every shape type regardless of dimension, which is the root of the LSP violation.

questionText: Given `interface Shape { double getArea(); double getVolume(); }`, why does `Line implements Shape` violate LSP?
option1: Line has too many fields
option2: Line doesn't use inheritance
option3: Line's constructor takes a double parameter
option4: Line is a 1D shape with no meaningful volume or area in the 2D/3D sense, so it can't honestly fulfill both methods of the contract — callers expecting a working Shape get broken or nonsensical behavior from a Line
correctOptionExplanation: LSP requires every subtype to honestly fulfill the base contract; forcing Line to implement getVolume() (or getArea()) it cannot meaningfully support breaks substitutability.

questionText: In the notes' diagram, `Line -> Shape` is marked with both a checkmark and an X. What does this represent?
option1: Line perfectly satisfies the entire Shape contract
option2: Line can fulfill part of the contract (e.g. length-like behavior) but fails another part (e.g. volume), so it is only a partial, unsafe substitute for Shape
option3: Line violates the Open/Closed Principle instead
option4: Line cannot be compiled at all
correctOptionExplanation: The mixed checkmark/X notation captures that Line satisfies some expectations of Shape but not others, exactly the kind of partial substitutability that breaks LSP.

questionText: Which of these is a typical way an LSP violation shows up in code for a forced method like getVolume() on a 2D shape?
option1: Making the method private so it's hidden
option2: Overloading the method with extra parameters
option3: Throwing an UnsupportedOperationException, returning a meaningless value like 0 or -1, or leaving the method empty
option4: Returning the exact mathematically correct volume
correctOptionExplanation: When a subtype can't truthfully implement an inherited method, common symptoms are throwing an exception, returning a dummy/incorrect value, or a no-op body — all silently breaking the contract callers rely on.

questionText: If code calls `shape.getVolume()` polymorphically on every `Shape` in a list that includes a `Circle`, what typically goes wrong under the single fat-interface design?
option1: Nothing, Circle naturally has a well-defined volume
option2: The code fails to compile
option3: Circle automatically becomes a Sphere
option4: The Circle either throws an exception or returns a meaningless value, silently or loudly breaking correctness for callers that trusted the Shape contract
correctOptionExplanation: A 2D shape has no real volume, so calling getVolume() on it exposes the LSP violation: the substitute (Circle) cannot honor the full base contract (Shape) safely.

questionText: What is the classic textbook example used to illustrate LSP violations involving rectangles?
option1: A Square class extending Rectangle, where setting width and height independently breaks Square's invariant that all sides are equal
option2: A Sphere class extending Cuboid
option3: A Circle class extending Line
option4: An Employee class extending Person
correctOptionExplanation: The Square-extends-Rectangle example is the canonical LSP case: Square must keep width == height, so overriding setWidth()/setHeight() to preserve that invariant breaks callers who expect independent Rectangle behavior.

questionText: Why does Square extends Rectangle typically violate LSP even though a square 'is a' rectangle mathematically?
option1: Because Square has more fields than Rectangle
option2: Because Rectangle is declared final
option3: Code that sets a Rectangle's width and height independently and expects the area to update accordingly breaks when substituting a Square, since Square must keep both sides equal
option4: Because Square cannot be instantiated
correctOptionExplanation: LSP cares about behavioral substitutability, not just conceptual 'is-a' relationships; Square's invariant (equal sides) conflicts with Rectangle's assumed independent width/height mutation.

questionText: What are the two fixed interfaces the notes introduce as a FIRST attempt to solve the fat Shape problem?
option1: IAreaCalculable (getArea) and IVolumeCalculable (getVolume)
option2: Shape1D and Shape4D
option3: AreaCalculator and VolumeCalculator
option4: IShapeReader and IShapeWriter
correctOptionExplanation: The notes show a first iteration splitting the fat Shape interface into IAreaCalculable (getArea) and IVolumeCalculable (getVolume), so shapes only implement what applies to them.

questionText: Under the first fix (IAreaCalculable / IVolumeCalculable), which interface(s) would Line implement?
option1: Both IAreaCalculable and IVolumeCalculable
option2: Only IVolumeCalculable
option3: Neither — Line doesn't cleanly fit area or volume calculation, showing this first attempt still isn't quite right for 1D shapes
option4: Only IAreaCalculable, forced awkwardly
correctOptionExplanation: The notes flag this first split as still imperfect for 1D shapes like Line, motivating the second, cleaner iteration with dedicated dimensional interfaces.

questionText: What is the SECOND, refined fix shown in the notes for the Shape hierarchy?
option1: One single interface with five methods covering every possible measurement
option2: Three interfaces — Shape1D (getLength), Shape2D (getArea), Shape3D (getVolume) — with each shape implementing only the interface matching its dimensionality
option3: A single abstract Shape class with all methods implemented as no-ops
option4: Deleting the Shape interface entirely and using raw classes
correctOptionExplanation: The final design in the notes segregates by dimension: Shape1D exposes getLength(), Shape2D exposes getArea(), and Shape3D exposes getVolume(), so each shape only implements what truly applies to it.

questionText: In the fixed code, `public class Line implements Shape1D { public double getLength() {...} }`. Why does this satisfy LSP where the old design didn't?
option1: Because Line no longer has a constructor
option2: Because Line is now declared final
option3: Line now only promises behavior it can honestly deliver (getLength), so any code using a Shape1D reference to a Line gets fully correct, expected behavior
option4: Because Line implements two interfaces instead of one
correctOptionExplanation: LSP is satisfied because Line's contract (Shape1D) exactly matches what Line can truthfully provide — full substitutability without broken or faked methods.

questionText: In the fixed code, `public class Sphere implements Shape3D { public double getVolume() {...} }`, the comment says 'No longer forced to implement getArea in a 2D context.' What LSP problem does this solve?
option1: Sphere can no longer be added to a List
option2: Sphere is no longer required to fake or misuse a getArea() method it doesn't naturally support as a 3D solid
option3: Sphere must now implement getLength() instead
option4: Sphere no longer has a radius field
correctOptionExplanation: By implementing only Shape3D, Sphere is freed from having to provide a nonsensical or dummy getArea() implementation, restoring honest substitutability.

questionText: With the fixed design, `AreaCalculator` operates on `List<Shape2D>`. Why can it safely call `shape.getArea()` on every element with zero instanceof checks?
option1: Because Java automatically converts any object to Shape2D
option2: Because getArea() always returns zero if not implemented
option3: Because List<Shape2D> can only ever contain one element
option4: Because every object in a List<Shape2D> is guaranteed by the type system to be a genuine Shape2D that can honestly fulfill getArea(), which is the essence of LSP-safe substitution
correctOptionExplanation: This is LSP working as intended: the calculator trusts the Shape2D contract completely, and every substitutable implementation (Circle, Square, Rectangle) honors that trust without special-casing.

questionText: A comment in AreaCalculator.java reads 'LSP Fixed - No instanceof checks anywhere... We trust every Shape2D to honour the getArea contract.' What does needing instanceof checks usually signal?
option1: A likely LSP violation, where the code has to special-case certain subtypes because they don't behave consistently with the expected base type
option2: That the code is well-designed and follows LSP perfectly
option3: That Dependency Injection is being used correctly
option4: That the class is using the Strategy pattern correctly
correctOptionExplanation: Needing instanceof/type-checking to handle subtypes differently is a classic smell that some substitutes don't honor the base contract uniformly — exactly what LSP aims to prevent.

questionText: Which of the following best states the formal behavioral idea behind LSP (beyond just 'compiles fine')?
option1: Subtypes must never override any inherited method
option2: Subtypes must have the exact same number of methods as their base type
option3: Subtypes must honor the same preconditions, postconditions, and invariants expected of the base type, so callers relying on the base type's contract are never surprised
option4: Subtypes must always be declared as interfaces, never classes
correctOptionExplanation: LSP is fundamentally about behavioral (contract) compatibility — preconditions can't be strengthened and postconditions/invariants can't be weakened in subtypes — not merely structural compatibility.

questionText: In Design by Contract terms, what is the rule about preconditions in an LSP-compliant subtype override?
option1: A subtype method cannot demand stronger preconditions than the base method it overrides
option2: A subtype method must always add more preconditions than the base method
option3: A subtype method must remove all preconditions entirely
option4: Preconditions are irrelevant to LSP
correctOptionExplanation: Strengthening preconditions in a subtype would reject inputs the base type accepted, breaking callers who relied on the base type's looser requirements — a classic LSP violation.

questionText: In Design by Contract terms, what is the rule about postconditions in an LSP-compliant subtype override?
option1: A subtype method cannot weaken postconditions the base method guaranteed — it must deliver at least what was promised
option2: A subtype method must always weaken postconditions
option3: A subtype must guarantee fewer results than the base type
option4: Postconditions are irrelevant to LSP
correctOptionExplanation: Weakening postconditions would mean the subtype delivers less than what callers were promised by the base type's contract, breaking substitutability.

questionText: Which real-world example is a commonly cited LSP violation: a Bird base class with a fly() method and a Penguin subclass?
option1: Penguin extends Bird and swims better, which is a valid LSP-compliant improvement
option2: Bird should never have subclasses at all
option3: Penguin extends Bird but can't actually fly, so overriding fly() to throw an exception or do nothing breaks code that assumes every Bird can fly()
option4: This has nothing to do with LSP, only with OCP
correctOptionExplanation: Like the Shape example, forcing Penguin to fulfill a fly() contract it cannot honestly support (throwing/no-op) is the same category of LSP violation as forcing Line to implement getVolume().

questionText: What is a good LSP-compliant fix for the classic Bird/Penguin fly() problem?
option1: Segregate the capability into interfaces, e.g. FlyingBird (fly()) and SwimmingBird (swim()), so Penguin only implements the abilities it actually has
option2: Make fly() throw a RuntimeException in Penguin and document it well
option3: Force every Bird subclass to override fly() with an empty body
option4: Remove the Bird class entirely and use only Strings
correctOptionExplanation: This mirrors the Shape1D/2D/3D fix: segregating capability-specific interfaces lets each subtype only commit to contracts it can truthfully fulfill, restoring LSP.

questionText: How does LSP relate to the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) in the Shape example?
option1: LSP and ISP are entirely unrelated and never intersect in practice
option2: Fixing LSP always breaks ISP and vice versa
option3: Splitting the fat Shape interface into Shape1D/2D/3D interfaces is an ISP-driven refactor that also fixes the underlying LSP violation by only requiring subtypes to implement what applies to them
option4: ISP only applies to abstract classes while LSP only applies to interfaces
correctOptionExplanation: In this codebase, segregating interfaces (ISP) is precisely what resolves the LSP violation, showing how the two principles reinforce each other in practice.

questionText: Does LSP only apply to interface implementation (implements) or also to class inheritance (extends)?
option1: It applies only to final classes
option2: It applies to both — any subtype relationship, whether via extends or implements, must preserve behavioral substitutability
option3: It applies only to abstract classes and never to interfaces
option4: It applies only to interfaces and never to abstract or concrete class inheritance
correctOptionExplanation: LSP is a general principle about any subtyping relationship, covering class inheritance (extends) just as much as interface implementation (implements).

questionText: If `AreaCalculator` were changed to accept `List<Object>` and use `instanceof Circle`, `instanceof Square`, etc. inside calculateTotalArea(), what design principles would this likely violate?
option1: Only encapsulation, nothing else
option2: Both LSP (special-casing types instead of trusting a shared contract) and OCP (needing to edit the method for every new shape type)
option3: Nothing, this is a completely valid and recommended design
option4: Only the Single Responsibility Principle
correctOptionExplanation: Type-checking each shape individually abandons the trust-the-contract behavior LSP relies on, and also forces edits for every new shape type, violating OCP as well.

questionText: Why is 'the subtype should never do less than the base type promises' a useful informal way to remember LSP?
option1: It captures that overriding methods shouldn't narrow behavior, throw unexpected exceptions, or return degenerate/meaningless results compared to what callers of the base type expect
option2: Because it means every subtype must return larger numeric values
option3: Because it means subtypes can never override base methods
option4: Because subtypes must always add brand-new unrelated methods
correctOptionExplanation: This mnemonic reflects the core of LSP: a substitute must be at least as capable and well-behaved as the base type promised, never quietly doing less or breaking expectations.

questionText: What real benefit does an LSP-compliant Shape1D/2D/3D design give AreaCalculator and VolumeCalculator when a new shape like Triangle is added?
option1: Triangle must implement both Shape2D and Shape3D to be added safely
option2: AreaCalculator must be rewritten with a new if-else branch for Triangle
option3: Triangle can simply implement Shape2D and immediately work correctly with AreaCalculator with zero changes to AreaCalculator's code, since every Shape2D can be trusted
option4: VolumeCalculator must also be updated even though Triangle is 2D
correctOptionExplanation: Because AreaCalculator trusts the Shape2D contract fully (LSP), any new, well-behaved Shape2D implementation like Triangle plugs in immediately without modification — this also demonstrates OCP in action.

questionText: Which of these is a subtle LSP violation even when the subtype technically overrides every base method?
option1: A subtype that marks its class as final
option2: A subtype that adds an extra constructor overload
option3: A subtype override that changes the meaning of the result (e.g. a Stack.push() subtype that silently drops items instead of storing them) while keeping the same method signature
option4: A subtype that implements an additional, unrelated interface
correctOptionExplanation: LSP violations aren't only about missing methods; they include semantically broken overrides that keep the same signature but silently change or corrupt expected behavior.

questionText: Can throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` from an inherited method ever be considered a valid LSP-compliant design choice?
option1: Rarely, and only if it's clearly documented as part of the type's contract everywhere it's used; in general it's a strong signal of an LSP violation, as seen in the original fat Shape interface
option2: No exception can ever be thrown from any method in Java
option3: Yes, always, since exceptions are a normal part of Java
option4: Yes, because exceptions automatically satisfy any interface contract
correctOptionExplanation: While Java technically allows it, silently throwing to reject part of an inherited contract (like the original getVolume() on Line) is the textbook symptom of an LSP violation the notes are fixing.

questionText: What does 'history constraint' mean in the formal definition of LSP (property changes over time)?
option1: It means subtypes must keep a log file of every method call
option2: A subtype shouldn't allow state-changing operations that a client of the base type wouldn't expect to be possible (e.g. making an otherwise-immutable base property mutable in a subtype)
option3: It means a subtype must be created before its base class in code
option4: It refers only to Git commit history of the class
correctOptionExplanation: The history constraint says subtypes shouldn't introduce new ways to change state that violate invariants clients could rely on in the base type, preserving predictable behavior over an object's lifetime.

questionText: In the notes, why is a `Cuboid` grouped with `Sphere` under `getV` and `getA` in the diagram (both listed together) while `Circle`/`Square` are grouped separately under `getArea` only?
option1: Cuboid and Sphere are 3D solids needing both area (surface area) and volume, while Circle and Square are 2D shapes needing only area — reflecting the real behavioral differences that the segregated interfaces must respect
option2: Because Cuboid and Sphere are the only shapes with constructors
option3: Because Circle and Square cannot be instantiated
option4: There is no meaningful difference; it was a random grouping
correctOptionExplanation: The groupings in the notes reflect real dimensional differences in what operations genuinely make sense for each shape, which is exactly the distinction the Shape1D/2D/3D redesign is built around.

questionText: What would be an LSP violation if a `ReadOnlyList` subclass overrode `add()` to silently do nothing instead of throwing an exception?
option1: Callers using the base List's add() contract would believe an item was added successfully when it silently wasn't, producing incorrect program behavior downstream
option2: This has nothing to do with LSP since add() still compiles
option3: This is perfectly fine since silent failures are always safer than exceptions
option4: It's only a problem if the list is empty
correctOptionExplanation: Silently no-op-ing a mutating method the base type promises to perform breaks the postcondition callers rely on, corrupting program correctness without any visible warning — a classic LSP violation.

questionText: Why is LSP often considered harder to verify automatically (e.g. via a compiler) than SRP or OCP?
option1: Compilers fully enforce LSP through the type system
option2: LSP only applies to private methods, which compilers ignore
option3: LSP is actually the easiest principle to check automatically
option4: LSP is about behavioral/semantic correctness (does the subtype truly honor the contract's meaning), which compilers can't check — only that method signatures match, not that behavior is consistent
correctOptionExplanation: A compiler verifies structural conformance (method signatures exist), but LSP requires semantic/behavioral conformance, which typically needs tests, code review, or design discipline to catch violations like the original Shape interface.

questionText: What test can help catch LSP violations during code review?
option1: Ask 'if I substitute this subtype wherever the base type is expected, does every existing caller still behave correctly and as documented?'
option2: Ask 'does this class have more than 3 fields?'
option3: Ask 'does this class have a constructor?'
option4: Ask 'is this class marked public?'
correctOptionExplanation: This substitutability thought experiment is the practical heuristic for spotting LSP violations: swap in the subtype and check whether any caller's assumptions break.

questionText: Overall, what is the main real-world payoff of designing Shape1D/Shape2D/Shape3D instead of one fat Shape interface?
option1: It removes the need for any interfaces at all
option2: It guarantees the code runs faster at runtime
option3: It reduces the total number of .java files needed
option4: Every shape type honestly fulfills its contract, so calculators and other client code can safely, polymorphically trust any object of the given interface without special-casing or risking broken behavior
correctOptionExplanation: LSP's payoff here is reliability: client code (AreaCalculator, VolumeCalculator) can trust the contract completely, enabling safe polymorphism without instanceof checks or runtime surprises.

questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes LSP from simple method overriding rules in Java?
option1: LSP is a Java-only concept with no meaning in other languages
option2: Java's compiler only enforces that overriding methods have compatible signatures and covariant return types; LSP additionally demands the overridden behavior stays semantically consistent with what callers of the base type expect
option3: Java's compiler and LSP check exactly the same things
option4: Method overriding is impossible unless LSP is followed
correctOptionExplanation: The compiler's checks (signature matching, covariant returns) are necessary but not sufficient for LSP; true LSP compliance is a semantic guarantee beyond what static type-checking can verify.
